H&P – Detailed

Consult Summary:
25-year-old male with 7-day history of sore throat followed by dry cough and mild exertional shortness of breath; symptoms fluctuating but overall non-progressive. No red-flag features elicited. Reassurance, symptomatic care, and sick note provided.

History:
• Sore throat began last week Thursday/Friday (≈7 days ago).  
• Dry, non-productive cough started 1–2 days later (Saturday/Sunday).  
• Exertional shortness of breath, mild wheeze, and vague chest discomfort started 3–4 days ago; no dyspnea at rest.  
• Cough is constant throughout the day; not worse at night.  
• Initial low-grade fever for first 3 days; now afebrile.  
• Intermittent headaches; none at time of consult.  
• Decreased appetite but no reported weight loss.  
• Denies hemoptysis, purulent sputum, sinus congestion, nasal symptoms, rash.  
• No recent significant travel; lives in UK (moved from US 12 years ago).  

Past Medical History:
• No chronic medical conditions.  
• No asthma, thromboembolic disease.  

Medications:
• None.

Allergies:
• Peanuts (reaction details not documented).  
• No known drug allergies.

Social History:
• Non-smoker (only minimal experimental use “once or twice”).  
• No asbestos exposure known.  
• Alcohol or other substances: not discussed.  
• Working; missed two workdays this week due to illness; requests sick note.

Family History:
• Mother: lung cancer.  
• No family history of thromboembolic disease reported.

Physical Examination:
• Not performed (video consult).  
• Patient denies palpable neck lumps.  
• Vitals not recorded.

Investigations:
• None ordered.

Assessment & Plan:

Issue 1: Probable viral upper respiratory tract infection / acute viral pharyngitis with associated dry cough.  
  – Reassured patient regarding benign course.  
  – Advised symptomatic management: paracetamol (dose/route/frequency not documented), adequate oral fluids, rest.  
  – Safety-net advice: seek in-person medical review if breathlessness worsens, new red-flag symptoms (e.g., hemoptysis, high fever, persistent chest pain), or no improvement within 4–5 days.

Issue 2: Mild exertional shortness of breath and wheeze.  
  – Currently mild; no red-flag signs elicited.  
  – Same safety-net advice as above; attend GP or emergency services if acute deterioration.

Issue 3: Occupational absence.  
  – Issued sick note for additional days off work.

General Plan: None beyond above.

Quality checks:

● Missing expected elements: vitals, objective physical examination, medication reconciliation (OTC use not asked), detailed allergy reaction, alcohol history.  
● Internal conflicts: Patient first said “No shortness of breath” then “Yes… shortness of breath” – conflict noted but later clarified as mild exertional dyspnea.  
● Transcript quality: Clear; minimal background noise; occasional overlapping speech.
